name: First Responders — Fire, EMS, Police, Crisis and Relief

stations.why: The case every responder shares: a casualty tagged and re-tagged as they change, with the crowd and the structure moving around you.

The first ten minutes of a residential fire: the 360, the report that puts a picture in every radio on the channel, the mode called out loud, and the accountability check that proves everyone who went in is still there.

The sector behind the fire where the crew itself is the patient: vitals read against a real release criterion, and a member held back for re-evaluation no matter who is asking for him back on the line.
A house prepped against embers on the wildland edge, with the trigger point that turns a hose lay into a pull-out call the instant the wind says so.

The call this whole series trains toward running as a team instead of a crowd: roles called on arrival, compressions that never really stop, and the swap caught before anybody has to be told the depth already went shallow.

A reversal that is not over at the first dose: rescue breaths that buy the time naloxone needs, a second stop in breathing caught before it becomes the story, and a bystander's own dose thanked instead of overlooked.

The call that starts before anyone is even out of the cab: the truck itself as the block, the light pattern that warns without blinding, and an agitated occupant approached from the one side traffic cannot reach.
The call where the words are the tactic: the approach slowed, one speaker, the gap held, time given, and a stabilisation unit at the end of it instead of a cell.
What the shift costs, four hours later: the signs named, the confidentiality rule said out loud with its limits, and the duty question kept out of the room.
Three services under one plan on a wet shoulder: the block upstream, the taper to the posted speed, a driver in shock kept out of the live lane, and the lane given back.
A first intake where the room, the permission and the pace all belong to the client, and the reporting limits are said plainly before a disclosure makes them urgent.
One call worked all the way through: asked directly, reflected back, planned together, the dispatch decision said out loud to the caller, and taken to a supervisor afterwards.
The unaccompanied visit, where the address, the check-in times and the word for send help are agreed before the car moves and the exit is taken on the plan rather than on the atmosphere.
The shelter opening before anyone can rest in it: a resident registered with privacy and care, a family kept together, and a fire alarm test that has to be answered as real.
The block swept from the street, buddied and clear of every downed line and gas smell, with a structure classified honestly and never entered to prove it.
Look, listen, link at the family assistance centre: practical needs met first, a person's own words reflected, and a reporter turned away from a family that never agreed to be quoted.

The wildland edge from the crew's own side of it: LCES named before a tool moves, and a wind shift or a spot fire across the line answered by the radio instead of by someone deciding alone to keep cutting.

summary: Stations for the people who run toward the call, with the human side scored as procedure: size-up and rehab on the fireground, cardiac arrest as a pit crew, an overdose reversed, a crisis call de-escalated, a critical incident debriefed, trauma-informed intake and a home visit, a shelter opened and a damage-assessment team sent out, and psychological first aid. Every station closes with the crew's own check-in and the peer-support line the department uses.
union: IAFF firefighters and EMS, NAGE and AFSCME EMS locals, police officer associations and the FOP, NASW and SEIU 1021 social workers and crisis counsellors, AFSCME and LIUNA disaster-relief crews with the Red Cross volunteer workforce
